papers.title: Groups of AI agents underuse resources despite shared evidence of increased capacity
papers.abstract: When AI agents share limited resources, such as computing services or public infrastructure, their individual choices affect how much work they complete as a group. Can sharing evidence of what is available let a group make full use of its resources after capacity changes? We tested this with language-model agents choosing between two simulated servers. One server recovered while its status report still listed it as unavailable. Each server had limited capacity per round, so rejected jobs required another attempt before the deadline. Telling agents that recovery was possible reduced missed deadlines. In controlled tests with Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, no agent tried the recovered server after a rule reminder, yet all chose it when shown a successful request record. After sharing, all five models tested left capacity unused. Keeping the success record fixed, we gave agents numbers without instructions, using each value equally often but giving group members either identical or distinct numbers. With OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol or Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, distinct numbers spread simultaneous requests across servers and increased job completions even though overall choice frequencies barely changed. Telling AI agents which resources are available leaves a second design challenge: helping them spread demand across those resources.

papers.title: Moral Inversion: Expressive Payoffs and the Reliability of Consensus
papers.abstract: Moral inversion is a public consensus on an account that falsely reverses responsibility for a harm. We study how expressive payoffs affect its emergence in a sequential social-learning model. A larger payoff makes an account more attractive to endorse, but also makes each endorsement of that account weaker evidence in its favor. We show that under a single-peakedness condition on private beliefs a larger payoff both increases the probability of an incorrect consensus on the favored account and reduces its reliability. Without this condition, both comparisons can reverse, and the informativeness of the public record can strictly improve in the Blackwell order. Finally, we show that a sufficiently large increase in the expressive payoff nevertheless restores the benchmark comparative statics.

papers.title: Does the AI Reviewer Alleviate or Aggravate the Maintenance Burden? Evidence from GitHub Copilot Reviewer
papers.abstract: This study examines how AI-based code reviewers reshape contribution behavior and maintenance dynamics in open-source software (OSS) communities. AI reviewers provide scalable, fast, and standardized evaluations. They reshape contributions as well as maintainers' workload. Leveraging the introduction of GitHub Copilot Reviewer on GitHub as a natural experiment in 2025, we investigate how AI review affects maintainers' workload and review efficiency as well as contribution behavior. We find that repository maintainers initially face a sharp increase in PR submissions and a higher review workload after the adoption of the AI reviewer. Over time, human contributions decline while the increase in bot-generated PRs is sustained. Interestingly, survival analysis reveals that AI reviewers increase review efficiency for human PR contributions, whereas bot PRs take longer to review and merge. Our findings suggest that while AI reviewers increase review efficiency, they aggravate the maintenance burden by encouraging more code contributions via humans and bots.

papers.title: Governance Risks in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs): Implications for Traditional Financial Institutions
papers.abstract: As financial institutions increasingly interact with blockchain ecosystems through decentralized finance, stablecoins, tokenized assets, and distributed ledger infrastructure, they come to depend on systems governed wholly or partly by decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs). This paper examines how DAO governance differs from traditional corporate governance and what this implies for risk management in regulated financial institutions. Using a qualitative comparative framework grounded in OECD governance principles, Basel Committee guidance, and FINMA circulars, the study maps DAO deliberation, voting, and accountability mechanisms against established governance and risk-management principles and illustrates associated risks through selected real-world cases. The analysis shows that DAOs preserve core governance functions but redistribute them across token holders, delegates, community forums, smart contracts, and legal wrapper entities. This creates distinct risks, including voting-power concentration, weak proposal controls, legal uncertainty, and unclear accountability, which established frameworks do not fully capture, while also offering two transferable strengths: a transparent, traceable decision record and a direct link between approval and execution. The paper contributes a structured assessment framework linking DAO governance characteristics to existing governance, outsourcing, technology-risk, and operational-resilience processes, enabling institutions to address DAO-governed dependencies through targeted extensions of current practices rather than a separate risk framework.

papers.title: Emergence and Collapse of Leader-Follower Flocks through Phantom Targets: Surprise Nullification in Bayesian and Inverse Bayesian Inference
papers.abstract: In Bayesian and inverse Bayesian (BIB) inference, a large prediction error can trigger surprise nullification, which expands belief and likelihood variances by a common factor, leaving the updated variance ratio the same as in standard Bayesian updating. This can increase belief uncertainty while keeping the learning rate low. In the simulations, three agents used BIB inference to predict one another's positions and moved toward those predictions, repeatedly forming leader-follower flocks that subsequently collapsed despite having no alignment rules or designated leaders. Three leadership criteria (front position, heading stability, and flock initiation) identified the same agent in 89% of eligible flocks, with different agents serving as leaders across flocks. Flocks formed when an agent nearly stopped incorporating another's observations (link cut) and moved straight toward a predicted position detached from reality (phantom target), thereby attracting followers. Link cuts arose when two successive resets assigned a very small and then an ordinary likelihood variance, sharply increasing the likelihood-to-belief variance ratio. Flocks collapsed upon link recovery or when returning phantom targets balanced the leader's forward and backward attractions. Without nullification, cuts persisted throughout the analysis period; expanding only belief variance caused recovery within a few steps. Expanding likelihood variance as well allowed cuts to persist while belief uncertainty grew, enabling later resets and recovery. Thus, nullification preserves relative precision, allowing cuts and flocks to persist, while reducing absolute precision to enable recovery and collapse, reconciling these seemingly opposing processes through a single operation. These results suggest that, in this model, individually inaccurate predictions can give rise to collective order.

papers.title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
papers.abstract: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

papers.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
papers.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

papers.title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
papers.abstract: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.
